title: Raga Kalyan
hook: the dishes are done, the lights come on, and the Granth turns to an evening raga that opens with a child and a parent

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Kanara, Guru Arjan's song of having no enemy and no stranger. Your line was no stranger. Whose face did you look at a second time? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-two.

The last plate goes in the rack. Somebody switches on a lamp. Outside, the streetlights have come on without anyone noticing the moment they did. The day's noise hasn't stopped, exactly, but it has moved further away, into the next street. A house in the early evening has its own sound: a kettle, a television low in another room, a child being called in. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga that tradition sings in this hour, as night begins. Its name is Kalyan. Today: Raga Kalyan, and the family picture it opens with.
screen: `THE LAST PLATE IN THE RACK.` → `THE LAMPS COME ON.` → `A RAGA FOR THIS HOUR.`

segments.voice: First, where we are. In the Granth's order, Kalyan comes right after Kanara, yesterday's raga, and its pages hold hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan. Tomorrow we'll read along with one of its hymns. Today, the door in. Tradition places Kalyan in the evening, in the first part of the night, and describes its mood as calm and settled. Teachers of raga describe moods in different ways, so hold that as tradition, not as a rule written in the Granth. What is written is the opening hymn, by Guru Ram Das. In paraphrase: no one has found the limit of the Lord who is in everything. We are your children; you are the one who looks after us. You are the great Being, my father and my mother. Notice what that first line does. It starts as big as it can: no limit, no end that anyone has reached. Then, in the very next breath, it comes all the way home. Children. A father. A mother. The infinite and the kitchen table, side by side. That's a fitting picture for the evening. Evening is the hour when children are called in, when the people who look after a house count heads and close the door. The hymn takes that ordinary scene and hangs the whole of creation on it. Whatever the day was, the one who sustains it is described as a parent. Peace, in this opening, isn't silence or emptiness. It's the feeling of a child who knows someone is watching the door. Sikhs who sing Kalyan in the evening sing it into exactly the hour when that picture is easiest to see. Today's line: peaceful evening.
screen: `AFTER KANARA: GURU RAM DAS, GURU ARJAN.` · `TRADITION: AN EVENING RAGA.` · `NO ONE HAS FOUND THE LIMIT.` · `WE ARE YOUR CHILDREN.` · then, large: `PEACEFUL EVENING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Kalyan, and let the day come in for the night. If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Kalyan; it doesn't need to be evening where you are. If you can't, sit in the quiet. Let the breath slow. Then, one by one, call the day's pieces in, the way someone calls children in from the street: the meeting, the errand, the thing you said too fast. Don't sort them. Just let each one come through the door, and let the door close behind it. If you pray, you can rest in Guru Ram Das's picture of the One who looks after us like a father and a mother. If you don't, simply let the house of your mind go quiet. The bell holds the time.
Raga Kalyan. The raga that follows Kanara, which tradition sings as night begins, opening with Guru Ram Das's hymn: no one has found your limit, and we are your children. Today's word.

Your line: peaceful evening. Tonight, when the lights come on, take one minute to do nothing but notice the house settling: the sounds, the people, who's home. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-two.
